# Conceptual framework {#sec-lit}

>This chapter presents the conceptual framework this thesis will use to understand the National Adaptation Plans.

As we saw in @sec-context, climate adaptation in being mainstreamed into development discourse. This makes it natural to look into the literature on development. This chapter will contrast the institutional- and critical approaches in the three central themes of the NAPs; implementation, financing, and knowledge production.

The first section presents the debates on how development projects interact with realities on the ground. Here, the te

The second section discusses how these projects are, and should be, financed. 

The third section, rather, the competing knowledge production paradigms. 

The last section presents some of the recent research on climate adaptation, especially in Bangladesh, and synthesizes the concepts into the adaptation nexus, the institutional approach, and the adaptation regime, the critical approach. 

## Implementation

>It is in the implementation that grand development theories meet local realities, and local peoples. This interaction has its own logics and adaptations. 

At its most basic level, it is about managing very large projects with a lot of unknowns, something very similar to megaprojects [@flyvbjerg2014;@flyvbjerg2023]. 

Historically, the institutional approach to development was through first the colonial state, and later the developing state. As the state fell out of favor, the NGO sector took over as the representative of the people one is trying to help [@banks2015]. The current institutional approach has increasingly embraced participation as its organizing principle, responding to decades of criticism about top-down, blueprint development. Participatory Rural Appraisal and its variants promised to revolutionize development by incorporating local knowledge, empowering communities, and ensuring that interventions respond to actual needs rather than perceived deficits [@chambers1994]. With the information, the communities were to be able to take action themselves [@freire1970]. 

What began as a radical critique of expert-driven development became a standardized toolkit that could be applied anywhere, transforming participation from a political process into a technical method. Participatory exercises, designed to produce information for the community to take action on their own, often served to gather information more efficiently than other approaches. The radical edge of the project, the empowerment of the local, was lost on the way [michael hadde en forelesning]. Rather than redistribute power, becoming new technologies of governance that extended rather than challenged existing relations.

The idea, then radical, now obvious, is that people are able and willing to live a better life. Lack either access [@ribot2003], capabilities [@sen2000], capital [@bourdieu2002] or aspirations [@appadurai2004] hinders them from achieving their potential. The addition of one of these, taken away by historical oppression, was thought to create a positive spiral. This approach has been common in many fields, such as agriculture/food security [@bingen2000;@fao2008;@wezel2020;@gibson2012] and human security [@undp1994;@chandler2008;@paris2001]. 

[expand on both, if needed]

Common for all approaches is that a social issue is seen as deeply connected to all others, and that there exists a room for outside intervention. The goal of the institutional approach is to find an efficient, scalable and sustainable intervention. To achieve this goal, frameworks such as the *Logical framework approach* (LFA) are commonly used [@ortengren2004]. These approaches also favor narrowly scoped problems, that are solvable through a straight forward intervention, with appropriate monitoring and evaluation.

The project format emerged as the dominant technology for organizing interventions, offering a framework that could travel across diverse contexts while maintaining bureaucratic coherence. Projects promise to make complex social realities manageable through logical frameworks that specify inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts in linear causal chains. Development institutions increasingly demand interventions that can be "scaled up"—successful pilot projects that can be replicated across regions, countries, or globally. What works in one context can work in another, that local success can become global best practice.

Critical scholarship on the implementation has focused on two aspects of the institutional approach. The first is that the local and their community, the beneficiaries, and protagonist in the institutional story, often is hard to find. The second is that the standardization of approaches makes political problems.

The *local* is also important to understand [@macginty2013;@macginty2015]. Local development brokers has also been a subject of study [@bierschenk2002;@lewis2006].

[expand on both, also if not needed]

The standardization of development approaches is, according to @scott1998, a necessary feature of centralized governance. Development interventions require making societies "legible" to administrative apparatuses creating standardized units, categories, and representations that enable measurement and control from a distance. This process also then removed a lot of the important information to govern societies, such as the present institutions [@lund2006;@bingen2000]. These institutions carry authority and legitimacy that is not easily replaced or subjugated, and can exist within, alongside or around the "formal" governance apparatus. 

This "rendering technical" of social issues, @li2007 argues that [to be continued]

Ferguson's concept of development as an "anti-politics machine" argues that development project fail in specific ways [@ferguson1994]. Development interventions consistently fail to achieve their stated goals, yet this failure does not prevent their reproduction. Instead, each failure generates new cycles of reform, new methodologies, new frameworks that promise to finally get development right. The development apparatus does not learn from its failures because the failures themselves are productive—they justify continued intervention while expanding bureaucratic power. By converting political questions about resource distribution and social justice into technical problems of project design and implementation, development depoliticizes fundamentally political processes.

## Financing

>Financing the gap is a central part of aid. But conditions apply.

While the section above dealt with the implementation of projects, the financing for these projects exist for themselves, in the global aid system. All aid is meticulously accounted in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) dataset for Official Development Assistance (ODA). The OCED Development Assistance Commite (DAC) maintains the taxonomies for the data, and makes it available through the Creditor Reporting System (CRS). This system is changed regularly, to better reflect the knowledge and policies of the OECD [@wp-stat2022;@wp-stat2020;@wp-stat2020a]. While the system is centralized, aid donors are responsible for reporting their own aid, according to their own conviction [@concitorapport]. 

The data is then used for two either research, or for donor countries reporting. It is through these taxonomies that the money pledged at COP (as discussed in @sec-context) are accounted. Here, the dollar amount could be written as loans, grants, or grant equivalent loans (loans given to a lower-than-market rate) and through NGOs, states or global funds [@kjaer2024]. Yet, over 70% of flows are from a donor state to a donor country, as grants, although around half is implemented by actors other than the government [@un2024]. 

This apparent contradiction, where aid formally flows between sovereign states but is often implemented by third parties, reveals a deeper complexity in the aid relationship. The seemingly straightforward bilateral transfer from donor to recipient country masks the extensive conditions that shape how, where, and for what purposes aid can be used. These conditionalities, which have evolved significantly since the structural adjustment era of the 1980s and 1990s, remain a defining feature of the contemporary aid architecture, effectively constraining recipient country autonomy despite the formal appearance of government-to-government cooperation.

The post-World War II international order established the sovereign nation-state as the fundamental unit of international relations and development. Decolonization created dozens of new states, each with flags, governments, and seats at the United Nations, embodying the promise that formerly colonized peoples could chart their own developmental paths. The institutional approach to development took this sovereignty as given, treating states as autonomous actors capable of making policy choices that would determine their developmental trajectories. International cooperation would facilitate technology transfer and capacity building between sovereign equals, enabling newly independent states to modernize and eventually join the ranks of developed countries [@escobar1995].

Mahmood Mamdani's analysis of the bifurcated state reveals how this structural dependency operates through inherited colonial institutions [@mamdani1996]. Post-independence African states maintained the fundamental structure of colonial governance: a modern civil law for urban citizens and customary law for rural subjects, creating a form of decentralized despotism that fragments resistance while facilitating extraction. The state simultaneously appears too present—in its bureaucratic and coercive apparatus—and too absent—in its failure to provide development or represent popular interests. This institutional inheritance ensures that even with African leaders, the state continues to function as a mechanism for managing populations rather than representing them.

Yet this formal sovereignty masked the continuation of colonial relationships in new forms. As Walter Rodney demonstrates, the very process of creating independent African states occurred within a framework that ensured continued exploitation [@rodney1989]. The wealth created by African labor and from African resources continued to be grabbed by capitalist countries, while restrictions were placed upon African capacity to make maximum use of economic potential. The presence of what Rodney calls "African sell-outs" became part of the definition of underdevelopment—local elites whose interests aligned with metropolitan capital rather than national development. Political independence without economic power meant that real decision-making remained centered outside national boundaries.

The concept of structural dependency emerged from Latin American scholars who observed that their countries' economies, despite political independence, remained oriented toward serving metropolitan needs rather than national development. Dependency theorists demonstrated that underdevelopment was not an original condition but actively produced through the relationship between center and periphery. Samir Amin's analysis extends this framework to show how aid itself becomes a mechanism of dependency, creating debt relationships that ensure continued subordination while appearing to promote development [@amin2009]. The aid system requires recipients to accept policy conditionalities, purchase donor country products, and orient their economies toward export markets, reproducing the very structures that create the need for aid.

This dependency operates through multiple mechanisms. Terms of trade systematically favor manufactured goods from developed countries over primary commodities from developing countries. When developing countries attempt to industrialize, they face technological dependency—relying on imported machinery, patents, and expertise that ensure continued flows of value to the center. Financial dependency emerges through debt relationships that require ever-greater proportions of national resources to service, creating what Yusuf Bangura calls "a vicious cycle of dependence and underdevelopment" [@bangura2010]. Even successful development within this framework often intensifies dependency, as countries become more integrated into global value chains controlled from metropolitan centers.

The conditions attached to the loans have changed over time, and the shock therapy model of post-socialist transformation offers a clear example of what the dominating thinking was at the time [@gevorkyan2018]. Like climate adaptation, economic transition was rendered as a technical challenge requiring rapid, standardized interventions based on best practices. The fact that the former Soviet Union spanned a massive territory and had multiple economic systems at the same time, the interventions were standardized and centralized. The results were to many catastrophic, some countries did not recover to the same living standards as was in the Soviet Union until 2015 [@gevorkyan2021a]. Yet the failures were attributed to incomplete or improper implementation rather than flawed frameworks, justifying further rounds of technical assistance and structural adjustment.

The rise of neoliberal globalization from the 1980s intensified these dependencies while transforming their character. Structural adjustment programs imposed by the World Bank and International Monetary Fund required states to liberalize their economies, privatize public assets, and reduce social spending in exchange for loans needed to service existing debts. These programs effectively restructured entire economies according to a universal template, eliminating policy space for alternative development strategies. The state's role shifted from developmental agent to facilitator of market access, managing populations to ensure political stability for investment while abandoning commitments to social welfare.

The financialization of development represents the latest transformation in these dependency relationships [@bernards2024]. Development finance increasingly operates through complex financial instruments—blended finance, green bonds, public-private partnerships—that promise to mobilize private capital for development goals. Yet as Nick Bernards demonstrates, this financialization often deepens rather than resolves dependencies. Developing countries must offer increasingly favorable terms to attract private investment, including guarantees that transfer risk from private investors to public institutions.

The sovereign state, rather than representing national interests against global pressures, often becomes the mechanism through which these pressures are internalized and enforced. States negotiate structural adjustment, sign investment treaties, and implement donor projects, appearing as sovereign actors while functioning as transmission belts for global capital. This produces what might be called sovereignty without autonomy—the formal apparatus of statehood without meaningful control over developmental directions. The state maintains monopoly over legitimate violence within its territory but lacks capacity to direct economic transformation or resist external pressures.

Alternative conceptualizations of development have emerged from recognition of these structural constraints. Scandinavian social democracy, as Kalle Moene argues, achieved development through social equality rather than following conventional growth models [@moene2016]. By ensuring broad distribution of productivity gains and maintaining full employment, Nordic countries created internal markets that supported industrialization without extreme inequality. Yet even this model depended on particular global conditions—small, homogeneous populations, strategic positioning during the Cold War, and ability to benefit from global trade while maintaining domestic social contracts—that cannot be easily replicated elsewhere.

The tension between sovereignty and dependency shapes how countries engage with climate adaptation. On one hand, adaptation appears to offer new policy space—countries develop their own plans, identify their own priorities, and implement context-specific responses. The principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities" acknowledges historical inequalities and promises support without conditionality. On the other hand, accessing climate finance requires conforming to donor frameworks, implementing standardized procedures, and accepting technical assistance that often reproduces existing dependencies.

This structural context helps explain the convergence documented in National Adaptation Plans. Countries face pressure to produce documents that will be legible and acceptable to donors, leading to adoption of similar frameworks, vocabularies, and approaches regardless of specific contexts. The apparent technical consensus masks how adaptation planning becomes a site where global power relations are reproduced. Countries must present themselves as vulnerable enough to deserve support but capable enough to manage funds effectively, technically competent but requiring capacity building, sovereign but open to partnership.

The financialization of climate adaptation threatens to intensify these contradictions. Proposals for innovative finance—catastrophe bonds, climate insurance, debt-for-climate swaps—promise to mobilize private capital while reducing aid dependency. Yet these instruments often create new forms of dependency, as countries become integrated into global financial markets on unfavorable terms. Insurance schemes require countries to pay premiums for coverage that may never materialize, while catastrophe bonds transfer resources to investors during precisely the periods when countries most need support. The technical complexity of these instruments creates dependencies on financial advisors, rating agencies, and international law firms, establishing new forms of rent extraction.

## Knowledge production

>

The question of whose knowledge counts in climate adaptation planning reveals fundamental tensions about expertise, legitimacy, and control in North-South relations. Climate adaptation emerges not as a neutral technical field but as a continuation of development discourse, inheriting both its institutional mechanisms for knowledge production and its epistemological hierarchies. Different approaches to understanding how knowledge operates in development and adaptation planning offer competing explanations for the patterns observed in adaptation discourse, from successful knowledge transfer to systematic epistemological control.

The contemporary architecture of climate adaptation knowledge production centers on international financial institutions, particularly the World Bank and regional development banks, which have established themselves as authoritative sources of expertise on vulnerability, resilience, and adaptation pathways. This institutional approach frames adaptation as a technical challenge requiring expert knowledge to identify optimal interventions, build institutional capacity, and transfer proven technologies from developed to developing countries. The World Bank's Climate Change Action Plan 2021-2025 exemplifies this vision, positioning the institution as a "knowledge bank" that collects, synthesizes, and disseminates best practices for climate-resilient development [@wb2021].

This expert-driven approach operates through what David Guston calls "anticipatory governance"—institutional arrangements that use technical knowledge to manage uncertain futures [@guston2014]. Climate models project impacts decades ahead, vulnerability assessments quantify exposure and sensitivity, and cost-benefit analyses determine optimal adaptation investments. These technical tools promise to make the uncertain future knowable and manageable through scientific expertise. National Adaptation Plans become exercises in translating this global expertise into national contexts, with countries required to conduct vulnerability assessments using standardized methodologies, identify adaptation options from established menus of interventions, and present results through frameworks that make their efforts legible to international funders.

The institutional production of adaptation knowledge operates through specific mechanisms that shape what can be known and said. Logical framework approaches require countries to articulate their adaptation needs through predetermined categories of inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. Results-based management frameworks demand quantifiable indicators of success that privilege certain types of interventions—infrastructure projects with measurable outputs—over others that resist easy quantification, such as strengthening traditional ecological knowledge or enhancing community solidarity. Economic valuation techniques transform complex ecological and social relationships into monetary terms, making adaptation decisions appear as technical calculations rather than political choices about values and priorities.

The institutional approach faces the challenge of reconciling universal frameworks with local specificities. While claiming universal applicability based on scientific knowledge, it must confront the irreducible specificity of climate impacts and adaptation responses. The same temperature increase produces fundamentally different effects in small island states facing sea-level rise, mountain regions losing glaciers, or drylands experiencing intensified droughts. The institutional response has been to develop increasingly sophisticated assessment tools and to incorporate "participatory approaches" and "indigenous knowledge" as inputs to planning processes, maintaining the central role of technical expertise while acknowledging local knowledge.

The post-structuralist critique of development knowledge fundamentally challenges these institutional approaches by revealing how expertise operates as a form of power. Drawing on Foucault's analysis of knowledge/power relationships, James Ferguson demonstrates how development discourse transforms political questions into technical problems requiring expert solutions [@ferguson1994]. In his analysis of development projects in Lesotho, Ferguson shows how development agencies systematically misrepresented local realities to fit predetermined intervention templates, depicting a commercialized economy integrated into regional markets as a traditional subsistence society isolated from modern economic life. This misrepresentation was not simply error but a necessary condition for development intervention—problems must be rendered technical to justify expert solutions.

Arturo Escobar extends this analysis in his examination of development discourse, arguing that development creates the very reality it claims to describe [@escobar1995]. The categorization of countries as "developed" or "developing," the identification of problems as "poverty" or "backwardness," and the prescription of solutions as "modernization" or "capacity building" construct a particular reality that makes certain interventions appear necessary and natural. Countries learn to see themselves through these categories, articulating their needs in terms that development institutions recognize and reward. This discursive power operates not through direct coercion but through the creation of subjects who internalize development categories and discipline themselves accordingly.

Tania Murray Li identifies specific mechanisms through which complex political problems are "rendered technical"—extracted from their political contexts and inserted into frameworks where expert knowledge can be applied [@murray2007]. Complex histories of land dispossession become issues of "unclear property rights." Political conflicts over resource access become problems of "weak governance." Structural inequalities in global trade become matters of "limited market access." Each translation strips away political content, transforming contested issues into problems with technical solutions. This rendering technical is not a conspiracy but emerges from the institutional requirements of development agencies that need to define problems they can address with available tools.

In climate adaptation, these dynamics manifest through the construction of "vulnerability" as a technical condition requiring expert assessment and intervention. Vulnerability indices rank countries according to their exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, creating hierarchies that determine access to climate finance. Yet as Jesse Ribot argues, "vulnerability does not fall from the sky"—it emerges from historical processes of colonization, structural adjustment, and unequal integration into global markets [@ribot2013]. By focusing on biophysical exposure and generic adaptive capacity, vulnerability assessments obscure these political-economic roots of differential impact.

Boaventura de Sousa Santos advances the concept of "epistemicide"—the murder of knowledge—to describe how certain ways of knowing the world are not simply excluded but actively destroyed through the imposition of supposedly universal frameworks [@santos2016]. Santos argues that Western modernity operates through "abyssal thinking"—a system of visible and invisible distinctions that renders certain forms of knowledge as non-existent. On this side of the line lies science, expertise, and rational planning; on the other side, traditional knowledge, local practices, and alternative cosmologies that are dismissed as belief, superstition, or folklore.

This epistemicide operates in climate adaptation through the privileging of scientific knowledge and technical expertise over other ways of understanding and responding to environmental change. Indigenous cosmologies that understand climate through reciprocal relationships between humans and non-human beings find no place in vulnerability indices. Traditional ecological calendars based on subtle seasonal indicators cannot be incorporated into climate models. Community practices of reciprocity and mutual aid that have enabled survival through past crises appear irrelevant to results-based management frameworks. These knowledge systems are not simply different but are rendered non-existent within adaptation planning frameworks.

Santos proposes an "ecology of knowledges" as an alternative to epistemicide—a recognition that different knowledge systems have different strengths and limitations, and that addressing complex challenges requires dialogue between different ways of knowing rather than the imposition of a single epistemology [@santos2016]. This does not mean relativism where all knowledge claims are equally valid, but rather a recognition that different knowledge systems operate according to different logics, serve different purposes, and reveal different aspects of reality.

Dipesh Chakrabarty's concept of "provincializing Europe" provides another perspective on epistemological diversity, arguing that European categories of thought have been universalized in ways that obscure their particular historical and cultural origins [@chakrabarty2009]. Concepts like development, progress, and modernization emerge from specific European historical experiences but are applied as universal categories for understanding all societies. This is not simply a matter of cultural imperialism but shapes the very possibilities for thought and action in non-European contexts.

Arturo Escobar's concept of the "pluriverse"—a world where many worlds fit—offers a framework for understanding epistemological diversity in relation to different ways of being in the world [@escobar2018]. Escobar argues that the current ecological crisis stems from the imposition of what he calls the "One-World World"—a singular reality defined by Western modernity that eliminates other ways of being and knowing. Different communities inhabit different worlds constituted by distinct relationships between humans, non-humans, and territories. The Zapatista concept of "a world where many worlds fit" captures this vision where different ontologies coexist without being reduced to variations of a universal template.

Walter Mignolo's work on decolonial options extends this analysis by examining how coloniality operates through the control of knowledge, being, and power [@mignolo2011]. The "darker side of Western modernity" is not simply exploitation and oppression but the elimination of other ways of knowing and being in the world. Decolonial thinking seeks not to reform existing systems but to build alternatives based on epistemologies and cosmologies that have been marginalized or suppressed by colonial modernity.

These perspectives connect to indigenous resurgence movements that assert alternative relationships with land, time, and more-than-human beings. As Jeff Corntassel argues, indigenous peoples maintain knowledge systems and practices that offer alternatives to state-centric and market-based approaches to environmental governance [@corntassel2021]. These are not romanticized returns to the past but contemporary practices that adapt traditional knowledge to current conditions while maintaining distinct epistemological foundations.

The field of critical futures studies reveals how the future itself becomes a site of epistemological struggle. Sohail Inayatullah distinguishes between predictive, cultural, and critical epistemologies in futures thinking [@inayatullah1990]. Predictive epistemologies, dominant in institutional planning, assume the future can be known through scientific methods—modeling, forecasting, scenario planning. Cultural epistemologies understand futures as expressions of deep cultural values and worldviews. Critical epistemologies examine how certain futures are rendered possible or impossible through operations of power.

Inayatullah's Causal Layered Analysis provides a method for examining how different levels of reality—from surface events to deep myths and metaphors—shape what futures can be imagined [@inayatullah2013]. In adaptation planning, the litany level focuses on climate impacts and technical responses. The systemic level examines institutional arrangements and resource flows. The worldview level reveals assumptions about development, progress, and human-nature relationships. The myth/metaphor level uncovers deep stories about vulnerability, resilience, and transformation that structure what responses seem possible or impossible.

Critical futures studies connects to what Luke Goode and Michael Godhe identify as the need to move "beyond capitalist realism"—the inability to imagine futures beyond current political-economic arrangements [@goode2017]. They argue that mainstream futures thinking, despite its emphasis on change and innovation, often reinforces existing power relations by limiting imagination to variations within current systems [@godhe2018]. In adaptation planning, this manifests as the assumption that future societies will maintain current institutional structures, economic relations, and development trajectories, requiring only technical adjustments to manage climate impacts.

Richard Slaughter's work on the "foresight principle" examines how human agency is constrained by technoscientific frameworks that present certain futures as inevitable [@slaughter2024]. The dominance of technical approaches to adaptation planning reflects broader patterns in how institutions colonize the future through claims to predictive knowledge. Alternative approaches based on different temporalities, values, and ways of knowing struggle to find expression within planning frameworks oriented toward technical prediction and control.

The operation of different epistemologies in development practice occurs through complex processes of translation and brokerage. Development brokers—consultants, government officials, NGO staff—mediate between different knowledge systems, translating between international frameworks and local contexts [@bierschenk2002]. David Lewis and David Mosse demonstrate that these brokers do not simply transfer knowledge but actively produce it through acts of translation that transform meanings, create new categories, and generate institutional facts [@lewis2006].

These processes of translation involve what Jean-Pierre Olivier de Sardan calls the encounter between "traveling models" and "practical norms"—the standardized interventions promoted by development agencies and the actual practices through which things get done in specific contexts [@olivierdesardan2017]. Development projects must navigate between institutional requirements for standardization and local demands for relevance, creating hybrid forms that satisfy neither fully but enable resources to flow and activities to proceed.

In adaptation planning, international consultants play crucial roles in producing National Adaptation Plans, bringing expertise in institutional requirements, planning methodologies, and successful examples from other countries. Their expertise lies not primarily in climate science or local adaptation practices but in the institutional knowledge of how to produce acceptable plans—what language resonates with funders, what formats meet requirements, what evidence carries weight in international arenas. This creates what David Mosse calls "policy as practice"—the continuous work of maintaining coherent narratives about development interventions despite messy realities [@mosse2011].

These different epistemological approaches offer competing explanations for patterns in adaptation discourse. From an institutional perspective, convergence around certain themes and approaches reflects successful knowledge transfer and the consolidation of best practices. The dominance of planning frameworks, vulnerability assessments, and institutional arrangements indicates that countries are adopting proven approaches to managing climate risks. Variations in discourse reflect different stages of institutional development and capacity for implementing sophisticated planning processes.

From a post-structuralist perspective, convergence reflects the operation of discursive power that shapes what can be said and thought within adaptation planning. Countries learn to articulate their needs through categories that international institutions recognize, performing vulnerability in ways that secure access to resources. The rendering technical of political questions about land, resources, and sovereignty transforms adaptation into a domain of expert knowledge where alternative approaches appear irrational or irrelevant.

From an epistemologies of the South perspective, convergence represents epistemicide—the systematic elimination of alternative ways of knowing and responding to environmental change. The imposition of universal planning frameworks destroys knowledge systems based on different relationships with territory, time, and more-than-human beings. What appears as capacity building is actually the replacement of diverse epistemologies with a singular framework that serves institutional rather than community needs.

From a critical futures perspective, convergence reflects the colonization of the future by technical prediction and institutional planning. The inability to imagine adaptation beyond current institutional arrangements forecloses transformative responses to climate change. Alternative futures based on different economic systems, governance arrangements, or human-environment relationships become literally unthinkable within frameworks that assume the continuation of existing structures.

These perspectives do not necessarily contradict each other but operate at different levels of analysis. The institutional focus on technical knowledge and capacity building, the post-structuralist attention to discourse and power, the decolonial emphasis on epistemological diversity, and the critical futures examination of temporal colonization all illuminate different aspects of how knowledge operates in adaptation planning. Understanding these different approaches provides the theoretical tools for analyzing what patterns in National Adaptation Plans reveal about the politics of knowledge in climate governance.

## Nexus and Regime

The different epistemological approaches to development and knowledge production crystallize into two competing frameworks for understanding climate adaptation: the adaptation nexus and the adaptation regime. These frameworks represent not simply different perspectives but fundamentally different ways of understanding what adaptation is, how it operates, and what it accomplishes. The adaptation nexus presents climate adaptation as a technical challenge that can be addressed through integrated planning, institutional development, and knowledge transfer. The adaptation regime reveals adaptation as a continuation of colonial relations that maintains dependencies, eliminates alternatives, and transforms political questions into technical problems. These frameworks structure how we interpret patterns in adaptation planning—whether convergence represents successful coordination or systematic control, whether standardization enables efficiency or enforces conformity, whether mainstreaming achieves integration or accomplishes assimilation.

## The Adaptation Nexus

The concept of the adaptation nexus emerges from institutional approaches that understand climate adaptation as interconnected with multiple development sectors and challenges. In this framework, adaptation cannot be addressed in isolation but requires integrated approaches that recognize linkages between climate, water, food, energy, and economic systems. The nexus approach promises to identify synergies, avoid trade-offs, and maximize co-benefits across sectors. A single intervention—improving irrigation infrastructure—can simultaneously enhance agricultural productivity, build climate resilience, increase water efficiency, and generate employment. This benefit-stacking makes adaptation investments appear remarkably efficient, delivering multiple development outcomes through integrated planning.

The mainstreaming of adaptation into development represents the operational expression of nexus thinking. As Morgan Scoville-Simonds and colleagues document, mainstreaming promises to embed climate considerations across all development sectors rather than treating adaptation as a separate domain [@scoville-simonds2020]. Agricultural programs incorporate climate-smart techniques, infrastructure projects include resilience components, health systems prepare for changing disease patterns, and education curricula address climate awareness. This comprehensive integration appears to ensure that adaptation becomes central to all development planning rather than an add-on to existing programs.

International financial institutions have embraced the nexus approach as it aligns with their institutional logics of efficiency, integration, and measurable outcomes. The World Bank's Climate Change Action Plan explicitly adopts nexus thinking, promoting "green, resilient, and inclusive development" that addresses climate change while advancing broader development objectives [@wb2021]. Climate finance mechanisms increasingly require projects to demonstrate co-benefits across multiple sectors, encouraging proposals that promise transformative impacts through integrated interventions. The Green Climate Fund's investment criteria favor projects that achieve both adaptation and mitigation benefits while contributing to sustainable development goals.

The technical tools of nexus planning—integrated assessment models, multi-criteria analysis, systems mapping—promise to optimize resource allocation across complex interconnections. These tools render visible the relationships between different sectors, identify leverage points for intervention, and calculate optimal investment portfolios. Countries developing National Adaptation Plans are encouraged to use these tools to ensure comprehensive coverage, avoid maladaptation, and maximize development co-benefits. The apparent sophistication of these technical approaches lends authority to adaptation planning, making it appear as advanced scientific management rather than political choice.

Yet the nexus approach faces fundamental challenges in practice. The promise of synergies often confronts trade-offs that cannot be resolved through technical optimization. Water allocated to urban areas cannot simultaneously irrigate rural fields. Land used for flood protection cannot also house displaced populations. Resources invested in sea walls cannot also fund social protection programs. These trade-offs involve political choices about whose needs take priority, yet nexus planning presents them as technical problems amenable to expert solution. The multiplication of objectives through benefit-stacking can obscure rather than clarify these fundamental tensions.

The operationalization of nexus approaches through development practice reveals additional complications. As Camelia Dewan observes in her ethnography of climate change adaptation in Bangladesh, development organizations add "climate change as a spice" to existing projects, rebadging traditional interventions with climate rationales to access new funding streams [@dewan2022]. Agricultural intensification becomes "climate-smart agriculture," microfinance becomes "adaptive capacity building," and infrastructure upgrades become "climate-resilient development." This rebadging maintains existing development approaches while creating an appearance of comprehensive climate response.

## The Adaptation Regime

Critical scholars advance the concept of the adaptation regime to describe how climate adaptation operates as a system of control that maintains and intensifies existing inequalities while appearing to address climate vulnerabilities. Drawing on Ferguson's analysis of the anti-politics machine and Escobar's critique of development discourse, this perspective reveals adaptation not as a response to climate change but as a mechanism for extending governmental and market control over populations and territories deemed vulnerable [@ferguson1994; @escobar1995]. The adaptation regime does not simply fail to address climate impacts—it actively produces new forms of dependency and dispossession while eliminating alternative responses.

Kasia Paprocki's analysis of adaptation in Bangladesh reveals how the adaptation regime operates through the construction of crisis narratives that justify radical interventions [@paprocki2018]. Bangladesh is portrayed as "ground zero" for climate change, facing inevitable inundation that requires massive infrastructure projects, planned relocations, and economic transformation. These crisis narratives create what Paprocki calls "threatening dystopias"—visions of catastrophic futures that can only be avoided through expert-led interventions. The urgency of climate threat overrides democratic deliberation, community consent, and consideration of alternatives. Adaptation becomes a state of exception where normal rules and rights are suspended in the name of climate emergency.

The regime operates through specific mechanisms that transform climate adaptation into opportunities for accumulation and control. Commercial shrimp farming is promoted as climate adaptation, providing saline-resistant livelihoods for farmers affected by sea-level rise. Yet shrimp farming requires capital-intensive inputs, export-oriented infrastructure, and integration into global value chains controlled by multinational corporations. Small farmers become contract laborers on land they once owned, dependent on volatile global markets and corporate supply chains. What appears as adaptation to climate change accomplishes the transformation of subsistence producers into wage laborers.

Infrastructure mega-projects justified by climate adaptation create similar dynamics of dispossession and accumulation. The construction of climate-resilient cities, coastal embankments, and economic zones requires massive land acquisition, displacing rural populations in the name of protection from future climate impacts. These projects concentrate benefits among urban elites and international contractors while displacing costs onto rural populations who lose land, livelihoods, and ways of life. The promised benefits of climate protection rarely materialize for displaced populations, who find themselves more vulnerable after adaptation than before.

The adaptation regime extends beyond specific projects to reshape governance systems and state-society relations. National Adaptation Plans require countries to conduct comprehensive assessments of climate vulnerabilities, establish institutional arrangements for adaptation planning, and develop monitoring systems to track implementation. These requirements create new forms of governmental knowledge and control, making populations and territories legible to state and international institutions in unprecedented ways. Communities that have managed environmental variability for generations suddenly appear as vulnerable populations requiring expert intervention and state protection.

International climate finance reinforces regime dynamics by creating new forms of dependency and conditionality. Access to adaptation funds requires countries to establish specialized institutions, adopt standardized planning frameworks, and submit to international monitoring and evaluation. These requirements shape national institutions according to donor preferences, creating parallel bureaucracies that respond to international rather than domestic accountability. The promise of climate finance creates powerful incentives for countries to present themselves as vulnerable in specific ways, performing climate victimhood to secure resources while obscuring local capacities and alternatives.

The patterns observed in National Adaptation Plans can be interpreted through either framework, leading to fundamentally different conclusions about what adaptation planning accomplishes. From a nexus perspective, the convergence around planning procedures, institutional arrangements, and integrated approaches reflects the successful diffusion of best practices. Countries are learning from each other, adopting proven frameworks, and coordinating responses to shared challenges. The dominance of procedural topics indicates that countries recognize the importance of robust planning processes for effective adaptation. Regional similarities reflect shared ecological and institutional contexts that shape appropriate responses.

From a regime perspective, the same convergence reveals the operation of governmental control that eliminates alternatives and enforces conformity. Countries must adopt standardized frameworks to access climate finance, perform vulnerability in prescribed ways, and submit to international oversight. The dominance of procedural topics reflects the bureaucratic requirements of international institutions rather than local adaptation needs. Regional patterns indicate the influence of development banks, consultant networks, and expert communities that shape what can be said and thought within adaptation planning. What appears as coordination is actually control, what seems like capacity building is really subjection.

These competing interpretations cannot be resolved through empirical analysis alone—they reflect different understandings of what adaptation is and should be. The nexus framework assumes that technical knowledge can identify optimal adaptation pathways, that institutional development enables effective implementation, and that international cooperation facilitates learning and resource transfer. The regime framework reveals how technical knowledge operates as power, how institutional development creates dependencies, and how international cooperation maintains hierarchies. Both frameworks illuminate aspects of adaptation planning while obscuring others.

The implications of these frameworks extend beyond academic analysis to shape practical possibilities for climate response. If adaptation operates as a nexus, then improving technical tools, strengthening institutions, and facilitating knowledge transfer should enhance outcomes. More sophisticated vulnerability assessments, better integrated planning, and increased climate finance should enable more effective adaptation. The convergence observed in National Adaptation Plans would indicate progress toward coordinated global response, with countries adopting proven approaches while adapting them to local contexts.

If adaptation operates as a regime, then technical improvements and institutional strengthening may intensify rather than address underlying problems. More sophisticated assessments create more elaborate forms of governmental knowledge and control. Better integrated planning extends bureaucratic power across more domains of social life. Increased climate finance deepens dependencies and disciplines countries into conformity. The convergence observed in National Adaptation Plans would indicate the successful operation of epistemicide, eliminating alternative ways of understanding and responding to environmental change.

Understanding adaptation as both nexus and regime provides analytical tools for interpreting patterns in National Adaptation Plans. The high degree of discourse centralization observed across all countries could reflect either successful coordination around effective approaches or systematic elimination of alternatives. The dominance of procedural topics might indicate recognition of planning importance or submission to bureaucratic requirements. Regional clustering could reveal shared ecological challenges or common exposure to institutional influences. The relationship between income level and discourse autonomy might demonstrate capacity constraints or dependency relationships.

These frameworks also illuminate what is at stake in adaptation planning beyond technical effectiveness. The nexus approach, despite its promise of integration and efficiency, may obscure fundamental conflicts and trade-offs that require political resolution. By presenting adaptation as a technical challenge amenable to expert solution, it depoliticizes questions about resource distribution, development pathways, and desirable futures. The pursuit of co-benefits and synergies can become a way to avoid difficult choices about whose interests take priority when genuine conflicts arise.

The regime analysis reveals how adaptation planning can become a mechanism for extending control rather than enabling autonomous response to environmental change. By requiring countries to render themselves legible through standardized frameworks, adaptation planning creates new forms of governmental knowledge that enable intervention and management. The construction of vulnerability as a technical condition requiring expert response undermines local capacities and alternative practices that have enabled communities to navigate environmental variability for generations.

Yet neither framework fully captures the complex realities of adaptation planning, which involves both technical challenges requiring expertise and political struggles over resources and futures. Real adaptation planning occurs in the space between nexus and regime, where technical requirements meet political pressures, where institutional frameworks encounter local realities, where expert knowledge confronts community experience. Understanding these dynamics requires holding both frameworks in tension, using each to illuminate what the other obscures.

The question is not whether adaptation planning represents nexus or regime but how these dynamics interact in specific contexts. When does integration enable more effective response, and when does it obscure necessary trade-offs? When does standardization facilitate coordination, and when does it eliminate valuable diversity? When does expert knowledge enhance local capacity, and when does it undermine community autonomy? These questions cannot be answered in abstract but require careful analysis of how adaptation planning operates in practice—analysis that the patterns in National Adaptation Plans begin to make possible.

Even ostensibly beneficial climate interventions can perpetuate colonial patterns and create new forms of dispossession. Carbon forestry projects in Uganda, funded by Norwegian, Swedish, and Finnish companies, have displaced thousands of farmers from their lands in the name of climate mitigation [@lyons2014; @mousseau2019]. The Green Resources company's plantations alone have affected over 8,000 people, destroying food gardens and grazing lands while promising carbon credits to Northern consumers [@mousseau2019]. Wind energy development in Oaxaca, Mexico, promoted as clean development, has been described as a form of "green colonialism" that continues patterns of indigenous dispossession through land grabs and violence [@dunlap2018].

These cases reveal how climate governance creates what Wilhite and Salinas describe as a "triple burden" on forest peoples in the Global South [@wilhite2019]. First, they bear the impacts of climate change despite minimal contribution to emissions. Second, they face displacement from mitigation projects like REDD+ and carbon forestry. Third, they must adapt to both climate impacts and the disruptions caused by climate interventions. This triple burden demonstrates how the technical framing of climate solutions obscures their political impacts on vulnerable populations.

The process of translating global adaptation policy into national contexts reveals how power operates through technical frameworks. As Roberts and Pelling argue, this translation is never neutral—it involves choices about what problems to prioritize, whose knowledge to recognize, and what futures to envision [@roberts2018]. National governments, in developing NAPs, must navigate between international requirements for accessing finance and domestic political pressures. They must render complex local realities into standardized formats that donors recognize while maintaining sufficient local legitimacy to implement plans.

Climate governance increasingly operates through experimentation—testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, identifying best practices for replication. This experimental approach appears scientifically rigorous and politically neutral. Yet experimentation is never neutral; it requires decisions about what to test, where to test it, how to evaluate results, and what constitutes success.

The selection of experimental sites reveals political choices. Vulnerable populations in developing countries become laboratories for adaptation technologies that might never be tested on privileged populations. The designation of Bangladesh as an adaptation laboratory, while justified by its climate vulnerability, also reflects its long history as a site for development experiments. From Green Revolution agriculture to microfinance, Bangladesh has served as a testing ground for interventions later promoted globally [@paprocki2018].

The "no regrets" philosophy that guides much adaptation experimentation reveals troubling assumptions. If landscapes are deemed doomed to climate impacts, any intervention that generates some benefit appears justified. If rural livelihoods are considered unviable, dispossession through climate projects becomes acceptable. This logic enables interventions that might be rejected under normal circumstances—forced migration, livelihood transformation, ecological manipulation—by invoking climate emergency [@ireland2010; @paprocki2018].

The proliferation of adaptation projects reveals both the power and limitations of the development apparatus in addressing climate change. In Bangladesh, described as "ground zero" for climate adaptation, the coastal zone has become a laboratory for adaptation experiments. International NGOs, development agencies, and research institutions test interventions ranging from salt-tolerant crops to floating gardens, from climate-smart houses to planned migration programs. Each project generates reports, evaluations, and best practices to be replicated elsewhere [@paprocki2018].

This experimental approach treats vulnerable populations as test subjects for adaptation technologies. The "Climate Smart House" built by WorldFish exemplifies this dynamic—a demonstration project equipped with every conceivable technical fix, from rooftop latrines to rain-fed fish tanks. Yet as one staff member acknowledged, "it's not for community replication, it's for the donors." The proliferation of colorful signboards across rural Bangladesh, printed in English for donor visits rather than local languages for community information, reveals whose audience these interventions primarily serve [@paprocki2018].

Popular interventions often reflect assumptions about desirable futures that may not align with local aspirations. Development practitioners assume that farmers want to leave agriculture, that rural life is inherently miserable, that urbanization and industrialization represent progress. Climate change provides justification for transformations already desired by development institutions—shifting from subsistence to commercial agriculture, from diverse livelihoods to wage labor, from rural to urban residence. When existing landscapes are deemed "not worth saving" due to climate threats, experimental interventions with uncertain outcomes become justified as having "no regrets" [@ireland2010; @paprocki2018].

The environmental dimensions of development reveal these dynamics with particular clarity. In West Africa, colonial and contemporary development policy has consistently misread environmental change, interpreting landscapes through assumptions about degradation and deforestation that contradict local experiences and historical evidence [@fairhead2003]. These misreadings are not simply errors but constitute what Fairhead calls a process of "depoliticisation," where ideas of objectivity support bureaucratic management while obscuring how different locations and ecologies respond to use in very different ways. Inhabitants who managed their own fallows, fire-setting, and pasture management have lost control to forestry officials, while being subjected to intensive programmes to educate them out of supposedly destructive land uses.

This depoliticization extends to the production of knowledge itself. Development institutions generate particular forms of discourse that simultaneously construct developing countries as specific kinds of objects of knowledge and create structures of intervention around those objects [@escobar1995]. The repetitive and standardized nature of development discourse—its reports, project documents, evaluations—creates a regime of representation that appears to describe reality but actually constitutes it in particular ways. Countries become bundles of sectors, populations become target groups, and complex histories become indicators of progress or regression along predetermined paths.
